grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ livre (book).
grammar.rule: "Livre" is masculine, so it takes "le". "Les" is the plural article — we only need singular here.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ maison (house).
grammar.rule: "Maison" is feminine, so it takes "la". "Le" is masculine, and "un" is an indefinite article (a/an), not definite (the).

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ chat (cat).
grammar.rule: "Chat" is masculine, so it takes "le". "La" is feminine, and "des" is the plural indefinite article.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ fleur (flower).
grammar.rule: "Fleur" is feminine, so it takes "la". Don't be tricked by the consonant ending — gender must be memorized, not guessed from spelling.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ stylo (pen).
grammar.rule: "Stylo" is masculine, so it takes "le". "La" is feminine, and "une" is an indefinite article.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct definite article.
grammar.rule: "Chaise" (chair) is feminine, so it takes "la".

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct definite article.
grammar.rule: "Garçon" (boy) is masculine, so it takes "le".

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct definite article.
grammar.rule: "Porte" (door) is feminine, so it takes "la".

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the father"
grammar.rule: "Père" is masculine, so "the father" = "le père".

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the table"
grammar.rule: "Table" is feminine, so "the table" = "la table".

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the brother"
grammar.rule: "Frère" is masculine, so "the brother" = "le frère".

grammar.stem: Why does "fleur" (flower) take "la" instead of "le"?
options: Because "fleur" ends in a consonant "r", and consonant-ending nouns are always feminine.
Because "fleur" is a feminine noun — noun gender is grammatical and must be memorized, and feminine nouns take "la".
Because "fleur" refers to something in nature, and nature words are always feminine.
grammar.rule: Noun gender in French is grammatical, not based on meaning or spelling patterns. You must memorize each noun's gender. Feminine nouns take "la".

grammar.stem: A student writes "le table". What is wrong, and why?
options: "Table" is feminine, so it needs "la" — the article must match the noun's gender, which is masculine (le) or feminine (la).
"Table" starts with a consonant, so it should use "l'" instead of "le".
"Table" ends in -e, which means it can take either "le" or "la" depending on the sentence.
grammar.rule: The definite article must agree with the noun's gender. "Table" is feminine, so it requires "la table". The ending -e does not determine gender by itself.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ école (school, f.).
grammar.rule: "École" starts with a vowel. Even though it's feminine (normally "la"), the vowel forces elision: "la" becomes "l'".

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ homme (man, m.).
grammar.rule: "Homme" starts with a mute h (h muet), which acts like a vowel. "Le" becomes "l'" to avoid two vowel sounds colliding.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ hôpital (hospital, m.).
grammar.rule: "Hôpital" has a mute h, so it triggers elision: "le" becomes "l'". The accent on the ô is a clue — it often signals a mute h.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article for ___ université (university, f.).
grammar.rule: "Université" starts with a vowel. "La" becomes "l'" through elision. Gender doesn't matter for this rule — both "le" and "la" become "l'" before vowel sounds.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct article for "ami" (friend, m.).
grammar.rule: "Ami" starts with a vowel, so "le" becomes "l'".

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct article for "église" (church, f.).
grammar.rule: "Église" starts with a vowel (é), so "la" becomes "l'".

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the tree"
grammar.context: arbre (m.) = tree. Arbre starts with a vowel.
grammar.rule: "Arbre" is masculine and starts with a vowel, so "le" becomes "l'". The tree = l'arbre.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the child"
grammar.context: enfant (m.) = child. Enfant starts with a vowel.
grammar.rule: "Enfant" starts with a vowel, so "le" becomes "l'". The child = l'enfant.

grammar.stem: Why does "le" become "l'" before "homme"?
options: Because "homme" starts with a vowel sound — the h is silent (mute), and French uses elision to avoid two vowel sounds colliding.
Because "homme" is an exception to the le/la rule and uses a special third article.
Because all masculine nouns starting with h use "l'" instead of "le".
grammar.rule: Elision happens because French avoids two vowel sounds next to each other. "Homme" has a mute h (silent), so the word effectively starts with the vowel "o". Not all h-words are mute — words with an aspirated h (like "le haricot") keep "le" or "la".

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article: ___ crayon (pencil, m.).
grammar.rule: "Crayon" is masculine, so the indefinite article is "un" (a pencil). "Une" would be feminine, and "le" is definite (the), not indefinite (a).

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article: ___ lampe (lamp, f.).
grammar.context: Il y a ___ lampe dans la chambre.
grammar.rule: "Lampe" is feminine, so the indefinite article is "une" (a lamp). "Un" is masculine, and "des" is plural (some).

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article: ___ jardin (garden, m.).
grammar.rule: "Jardin" is masculine, so it takes "un" (a garden). "Une" is feminine indefinite, "la" is feminine definite.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct article: ___ robe (dress, f.).
grammar.rule: "Robe" is feminine, so it takes "une" (a dress). "Un" is masculine indefinite, and "l'" is a definite article before vowels.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct indefinite article for "chien" (dog, m.).
grammar.rule: "Chien" is masculine: a dog = un chien.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct indefinite article for "fenêtre" (window, f.).
grammar.rule: "Fenêtre" is feminine: a window = une fenêtre.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a bag"
grammar.rule: "Sac" is masculine, so a bag = un sac.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a car"
grammar.rule: "Voiture" is feminine, so a car = une voiture.

grammar.stem: What determines whether you use "un" or "une" for a noun?
options: The meaning of the noun — "un" for people and animals, "une" for objects and places.
The first letter of the noun — "un" before consonants, "une" before vowels.
The grammatical gender of the noun — masculine nouns take "un", feminine nouns take "une".
grammar.rule: Just like le/la, the indefinite articles un/une are determined by the noun's grammatical gender. Masculine = un, feminine = une. This has nothing to do with meaning or first letter.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "château" (castle)?
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -eau add -x for the plural: château → châteaux. Don't apply the regular -s rule or the -al → -aux pattern here.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "animal"?
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -al change to -aux: animal → animaux. Don't just add -s (that's the English pattern) or confuse this with the -eau rule.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "bras" (arm)?
grammar.rule: Nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z don't change in the plural: bras → bras. The article "les" is what signals plurality.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "jeu" (game)?
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -eu add -x: jeu → jeux. Don't add -s (rule 1) or confuse with the -eau → -eaux pattern.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "chat" (cat)?
grammar.rule: Most nouns simply add -s for the plural: chat → chats. The -aux and -eaux patterns only apply to nouns ending in -al and -eau.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "oeil" (eye)?
grammar.rule: "Oeil" is irregular: its plural is "yeux" — a completely different word. This must be memorized.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "oiseau" (bird)?
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -eau add -x: oiseau → oiseaux. Don't apply the regular -s rule.

grammar.stem: Which article replaces "un" in the plural?
grammar.rule: The indefinite article "un/une" becomes "des" (some) in the plural. "Les" is the plural of the definite article "le/la". "Uns" does not exist as an article.

grammar.stem: Write the plural of "cheval" (horse).
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -al change to -aux: cheval → chevaux.

grammar.stem: Write the plural of "nez" (nose).
grammar.rule: Nouns already ending in -z don't change: nez → nez. The article "les" shows it's plural.

grammar.stem: Write the plural of "gâteau" (cake).
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -eau add -x: gâteau → gâteaux.

grammar.stem: Write the plural of "feu" (fire).
grammar.rule: Nouns ending in -eu add -x: feu → feux.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the birds"
grammar.context: oiseau (m.) = bird. Plural of -eau nouns: add -x. Plural definite article: les.
grammar.rule: Oiseau → oiseaux (-eau adds -x). The plural article is "les": the birds = les oiseaux.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the newspapers"
grammar.context: journal (m.) = newspaper. Plural of -al nouns: -al → -aux. Plural definite article: les.
grammar.rule: Journal → journaux (-al changes to -aux). The newspapers = les journaux.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "some games"
grammar.context: jeu (m.) = game. Plural of -eu nouns: add -x. Plural indefinite article: des.
grammar.rule: Jeu → jeux (-eu adds -x). The plural of "un" is "des": some games = des jeux.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "the coats"
grammar.context: manteau (m.) = coat. Plural of -eau nouns: add -x. Plural definite article: les.
grammar.rule: Manteau → manteaux (-eau adds -x). The coats = les manteaux.

grammar.stem: Why does "journal" become "journaux" instead of "journals"?
options: Because "journal" is an irregular noun and its plural must be memorized individually.
Because all French nouns ending in a consonant change their ending to -aux in the plural.
Because nouns ending in -al have their own plural pattern: -al changes to -aux.
grammar.rule: The -al → -aux change is a systematic pattern, not an irregularity. It applies to most -al nouns: journal → journaux, animal → animaux, cheval → chevaux.

grammar.stem: Why does "nez" (nose) stay the same in the plural?
options: Because "nez" is a body part, and body parts never change form in the plural.
Because "nez" is irregular and has no plural form at all.
Because nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z don't add anything — they already "look" plural.
grammar.rule: French doesn't stack plural endings. Since -s, -x, and -z already mark the end of plural nouns, words that already have them don't change. The article "les" signals the plural instead.

grammar.stem: Why do the articles change from "le/la" to "les" in the plural?
options: "Les" means "some" and replaces le/la when there is more than one.
Because the definite article must agree in number with the noun — singular le/la becomes plural les.
Because le and la can only appear with singular verbs, so les is needed for plural sentences.
grammar.rule: The article must match the noun in number. Singular: le (m.) / la (f.). Plural: les (for both genders). "Les" means "the" (plural), not "some" — that's "des".

grammar.stem: Which is the correct way to say "the intelligent student" (f.)?
grammar.rule: The adjective goes AFTER the noun in French: l'étudiante intelligente. Option B has English word order, and option C has wrong gender agreement.

grammar.stem: Which is the correct way to say "an interesting book"?
grammar.rule: Adjective after the noun: un livre intéressant. Option A uses English word order, and option B has feminine agreement (-e) on a masculine noun.

grammar.stem: Which is the correct way to say "a difficult exam"?
grammar.rule: Adjective after the noun: un examen difficile. Option A uses English order. Option C uses the wrong article — "examen" is masculine.

grammar.stem: Which is the correct way to say "a French woman"?
grammar.rule: Adjective after noun + feminine agreement: une femme française. Option B has English word order. Option C has wrong article and no feminine -e on the adjective.

grammar.stem: Put the words in correct French order: "a red flower" → une ___ ___
grammar.rule: Adjective after the noun: une fleur rouge (a flower red).

grammar.stem: Put the words in correct French order: "a fast car" → une ___ ___
grammar.rule: Adjective after the noun: une voiture rapide (a car fast).

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "an American man"
grammar.context: homme (m.) = man, américain = American. Remember: adjective goes after the noun.
grammar.rule: Adjective after the noun: un homme américain.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "an important letter"
grammar.context: lettre (f.) = letter, important(e) = important. Remember: adjective after noun + gender agreement.
grammar.rule: Adjective after noun with feminine agreement: une lettre importante. "Lettre" is feminine, so "important" becomes "importante".

grammar.stem: Why is "un livre intéressant" correct and not "un intéressant livre"?
options: Because in French, most adjectives are placed AFTER the noun — the opposite of English word order.
Because "intéressant" is too long to go before the noun — short adjectives can go before.
Because adjectives only go before the noun when they describe colors.
grammar.rule: This is a fundamental word-order difference between French and English. In French, most adjectives follow the noun. Length and type don't determine position — it's the default grammar rule.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "content" (happy)?
grammar.rule: Add -e to the masculine form: content → contente. Don't leave it unchanged (that's for adjectives already ending in -e) and don't change the stem.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "fort" (strong)?
grammar.rule: Add -e: fort → forte. "Fortes" would be feminine PLURAL. Leaving it as "fort" skips the required gender agreement.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "triste" (sad)?
grammar.rule: "Triste" already ends in -e, so it stays the same for feminine. No double-e, no accent change.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "français" (French)?
grammar.rule: Add -e: français → française. "Françoise" is a woman's name, not the adjective form. Leaving it as "français" skips gender agreement.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine form of "intelligent".
grammar.rule: Add -e: intelligent → intelligente.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine form of "sincère" (sincere).
grammar.rule: "Sincère" already ends in -e, so it does not change for the feminine.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a tall woman"
grammar.context: femme = woman, grand = tall. Adjective goes after noun and must agree in gender.
grammar.rule: Add -e for feminine: grand → grande. A tall woman = une femme grande.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a shy girl"
grammar.context: fille = girl, timide = shy. "Timide" already ends in -e.
grammar.rule: "Timide" already ends in -e, so it stays the same: une fille timide.

grammar.stem: Why does "grand" become "grande" when describing a feminine noun?
options: Because "grande" is a completely separate word that means "tall" for women.
Because French adjectives must agree in gender with the noun they describe — adding -e marks the feminine form.
Because adding -e makes the pronunciation softer, which is traditionally used for feminine nouns.
grammar.rule: Gender agreement is a core rule: the adjective must match the noun's gender. Adding -e is the standard way to form the feminine of most adjectives. It's not a separate word or about sound preference — it's grammatical agreement.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "heureux" (happy)?
grammar.rule: Pattern A: -eux → -euse. The x drops and is replaced by s + e: heureux → heureuse. You can't just add -e to the -x ending.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "sérieux" (serious)?
grammar.rule: Pattern A: -eux → -euse. Sérieux → sérieuse. The same pattern as heureux → heureuse.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "actif" (active)?
grammar.rule: Pattern B: -if → -ive. The f voices to v (like knife → knives in English): actif → active. Don't just add -e to the f.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "sportif" (sporty/athletic)?
grammar.rule: Pattern B: -if → -ive. Sportif → sportive. The f-to-v voicing is consistent across all -if adjectives.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "premier" (first)?
grammar.rule: Pattern C: -er → -ère. Premier → première. The accent changes from no accent to grave accent (è), opening the vowel sound from "ay" to "air".

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "dernier" (last)?
grammar.rule: Pattern C: -er → -ère. Dernier → dernière. Same pattern as premier → première.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "bon" (good)?
grammar.rule: Pattern D: Double the final consonant + e. Bon → bonne. The n doubles to preserve the nasal vowel sound. "Bone" would change the pronunciation.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine of "italien" (Italian)?
grammar.rule: Pattern D: Double the final consonant + e. Italien → italienne. The n doubles before the -e is added.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine of "généreux" (generous).
grammar.rule: Pattern A: -eux → -euse. Généreux → généreuse.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine of "créatif" (creative).
grammar.rule: Pattern B: -if → -ive. Créatif → créative.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine of "étranger" (foreign).
grammar.rule: Pattern C: -er → -ère. Étranger → étrangère.

grammar.stem: Write the feminine of "naturel" (natural).
grammar.rule: Pattern D: Double the final consonant + e. Naturel → naturelle. The l doubles before -e.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a curious woman"
grammar.context: femme = woman, curieux = curious (m.). Pattern: -eux → -euse for feminine.
grammar.rule: Curieux → curieuse (Pattern A). A curious woman = une femme curieuse.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "an attentive student" (f.)
grammar.context: étudiante = student (f.), attentif = attentive (m.). Pattern: -if → -ive for feminine.
grammar.rule: Attentif → attentive (Pattern B). An attentive student (f.) = une étudiante attentive.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "an expensive dress"
grammar.context: robe (f.) = dress, cher = expensive/dear (m.). Pattern: -er → -ère for feminine.
grammar.rule: Cher → chère (Pattern C). An expensive dress = une robe chère.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a kind girl"
grammar.context: fille = girl, gentil = kind/nice (m.). Pattern: double consonant + e for feminine.
grammar.rule: Gentil → gentille (Pattern D, l doubles). A kind girl = une fille gentille.

grammar.stem: Why does "heureux" become "heureuse" and not "heureuxe"?
options: Because you always remove the last letter of an adjective before adding -e for the feminine.
Because -eux adjectives follow their own pattern: the x drops, s replaces it, and -e is added — giving -euse.
Because -eux is already a feminine ending, so only minor spelling adjustment is needed.
grammar.rule: The -eux → -euse pattern is specific to adjectives ending in -eux. The x cannot just take an -e (that would be unpronounceable). Instead, x becomes s, then -e is added.

grammar.stem: Why does "actif" become "active" and not "actife"?
options: Because -if adjectives follow Pattern B: the f "voices" to v, then -e is added — like English knife → knives.
Because f and v are interchangeable in French, so either "actife" or "active" is technically correct.
Because -if endings always drop the f completely before adding -e.
grammar.rule: The f-to-v change is called "voicing" — the sound moves from voiceless (f) to voiced (v). This mirrors the English pattern (knife/knives, wife/wives). The f doesn't drop entirely; it transforms.

grammar.stem: Why does "bon" become "bonne" (doubling the n) instead of "bone"?
options: Because "bon" is completely irregular and its feminine must be memorized — there is no pattern.
Because all short adjectives (one syllable) double their final letter before adding -e.
Because doubling the n preserves the vowel sound — without the double n, "bone" would change the pronunciation of the "o".
grammar.rule: The consonant doubling protects the preceding vowel sound. In "bon", the nasal vowel "on" would be lost if you just added -e (compare "bone" vs "bonne"). The double consonant keeps the original pronunciation intact.

grammar.stem: What is the correct plural? "Les garçons sont ___." (intelligent)
grammar.rule: Add -s for plural: intelligent → intelligents. "Intelligentes" would be feminine plural, but "garçons" is masculine.

grammar.stem: What is the correct plural? "Les filles sont ___." (contente)
grammar.rule: Feminine plural: add -s to the feminine form. Contente → contentes. "Contents" would be masculine plural — wrong gender.

grammar.stem: What is the correct plural? "Les hommes sont ___." (heureux)
grammar.rule: "Heureux" already ends in -x, so it doesn't change in the masculine plural. "Heureuses" would be feminine plural.

grammar.stem: What is the correct plural? "Les hommes sont ___." (français)
grammar.rule: "Français" already ends in -s, so it doesn't change for masculine plural. "Françaises" would be feminine plural.

grammar.stem: "Un homme et une femme" are both happy. The adjective form is:
grammar.rule: Mixed-gender groups use the MASCULINE plural form. Homme (m.) + femme (f.) = masculine plural "contents". Masculine wins in mixed groups.

grammar.stem: "La mère et la fille" are both tired (fatigué). The adjective form is:
grammar.rule: All-feminine group uses the feminine plural: fatiguée → fatiguées. "Fatigués" would be masculine plural. "Fatiguée" is feminine singular.

grammar.stem: Write the correct adjective form of "noir" (black) for: "Les chats sont ___."
grammar.rule: Masculine plural: add -s. Noir → noirs.

grammar.stem: Write the correct adjective form of "vert" (green) for: "Les robes sont ___."
grammar.rule: "Robes" is feminine plural. Vert → verte (feminine) → vertes (feminine plural).

grammar.stem: Write the correct adjective form of "américain" for: "Le frère et la soeur sont ___."
grammar.context: Le frère et la soeur sont ___.
grammar.rule: Mixed group (m. + f.) → masculine plural: américain → américains. Masculine wins in mixed groups.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The flowers are red."
grammar.context: fleur (f.) = flower, rouge = red. Plural of "la" is "les". Adjective must agree in number.
grammar.rule: Fleur → fleurs (add -s). Rouge → rouges (add -s). Les fleurs sont rouges.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The men are serious."
grammar.context: homme (m.) = man, sérieux = serious. Remember: -x ending adjectives in plural.
grammar.rule: "Sérieux" already ends in -x, so no change for masculine plural: Les hommes sont sérieux.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The girls are active."
grammar.context: fille (f.) = girl, actif = active (m.). Feminine form: actif → active. Then add plural -s.
grammar.rule: Feminine form: actif → active. Feminine plural: active → actives. Les filles sont actives.

grammar.stem: Why does "heureux" stay "heureux" in the masculine plural?
options: Because -eux adjectives only change in the feminine form, never in the plural.
Because adjectives ending in -x (or -s) already have a plural-sounding ending, so nothing is added.
Because "heureux" is an irregular adjective that has no plural form.
grammar.rule: Just like nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z, adjectives with these endings don't add -s for the plural — they already end in a letter that marks plurality. "Heureux" does have a feminine plural form though: heureuses.

grammar.stem: "Un garçon et une fille sont intelligents." Why is the adjective masculine plural?
options: Because the adjective always agrees with whichever noun comes first in the sentence.
Because French defaults to masculine for mixed-gender groups — if any noun in the group is masculine, the adjective takes masculine plural.
Because "intelligents" is the only valid plural form — "intelligentes" does not exist.
grammar.rule: When a group contains both masculine and feminine nouns, French defaults to the masculine plural form. This is called "le masculin l'emporte" (masculine wins). "Intelligentes" does exist — but only for all-feminine groups.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "bleu"?
grammar.rule: Bleu follows the regular pattern: add -e for feminine → bleue. It does not use -euse or stay unchanged.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "blanc"?
grammar.rule: Blanc is irregular: the feminine form is "blanche" (not "blance"). This is a common trap — the -c changes to -che.

grammar.stem: Which form of "orange" is correct for "les chaussures ___ (orange)"?
grammar.rule: Orange is an INVARIABLE color — it NEVER changes. No -s for plural, no -e for feminine. Les chaussures orange.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "un stylo vert"?
grammar.rule: Vert is a regular color adjective. Masculine plural: add -s → verts. "Vertes" would be feminine plural.

grammar.stem: Which sentence is correct?
grammar.rule: Marron is INVARIABLE — it never takes -s, -e, or -es. No matter the gender or number: marron stays marron.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of the color adjective.
grammar.rule: Vert is regular: feminine form adds -e → verte. Porte is feminine, so the adjective must agree.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of the color adjective.
grammar.rule: Gris already ends in -s. Masculine plural of gris stays gris — words ending in -s don't add another -s.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of the color adjective.
grammar.rule: Violet is irregular: feminine is violette (double -t + -e). Fleur is feminine, and les fleurs is plural → violettes.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of the color adjective.
grammar.rule: Jaune ends in silent -e, so it's the same for masculine and feminine. Singular feminine: jaune (no change). Color adjective goes after the noun.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The gray cat (f.)"
grammar.context: chat/chatte = cat, gris(e) = gray. Remember gender agreement and adjective position.
grammar.rule: Feminine of chat is chatte. Gris → grise (add -e for feminine). Color adjective goes after the noun: la chatte grise.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The white houses"
grammar.context: maison (f.) = house, blanc/blanche = white. Apply gender + plural agreement.
grammar.rule: Maison is feminine: blanc → blanche. Plural: blanche → blanches. Les maisons blanches.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The red roses"
grammar.context: rose (f.) = rose (the flower), rouge = red. Both the noun and color end in -e.
grammar.rule: Rouge ends in silent -e: same for masculine and feminine. Plural: add -s → rouges. Les roses rouges.

grammar.stem: Why does "marron" stay "marron" in "les yeux marron" (brown eyes)?
options: Because "marron" is an invariable color — it comes from a noun (the chestnut) and NEVER changes for gender or number.
Because "yeux" is an irregular noun, so its adjectives don't agree.
Because "marron" already ends in -on, which is a natural plural ending.
grammar.rule: Marron comes from the noun "marron" (chestnut). Colors derived from nouns (marron, orange) are invariable — they never take -e, -s, or -es. This is different from regular color adjectives like bleu or vert.

grammar.stem: Why is the feminine of "blanc" written "blanche" and not "blance"?
options: Because "blanc" is completely irregular and the feminine must be memorized.
Because adjectives ending in -c form their feminine by changing -c to -che (blanc→blanche, sec→sèche, franc→franche).
Because all color adjectives double their final consonant before adding -e.
grammar.rule: The -c → -che pattern is a specific French rule. Blanc→blanche, sec→sèche, franc→franche. It's not random — it follows a consonant-shift pattern. Not all colors double their consonant; this is specific to -c endings.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct form: "un ___ homme" (an old man).
grammar.rule: "Homme" starts with a vowel sound (the h is mute). Before a vowel or mute-h, use "vieil" (not "vieux"). "Vieille" is feminine and wrong here because homme is masculine.

grammar.stem: Choose the correct form: "un ___ appartement" (a beautiful apartment).
grammar.rule: "Appartement" starts with a vowel. Before a vowel or mute-h, use "bel" (not "beau"). "Belle" is feminine. The pattern: beau (consonant) / bel (vowel) / belle (feminine).

grammar.stem: What does "un ancien professeur" mean?
grammar.rule: Position changes meaning: "ancien" BEFORE the noun = former. "Ancien" AFTER the noun = very old/ancient. "Un ancien professeur" = a former professor. "Un professeur ancien" = a very old professor.

grammar.stem: Which is correct? "She has beautiful dresses."
grammar.rule: In formal French, "des" becomes "de" before a preceding adjective: de belles robes (not "des belles robes"). The adjective must still agree in gender/number: belles (fem pl).

grammar.stem: Choose the correct form: "un ___ garçon" (a new boy).
grammar.rule: "Garçon" starts with a consonant, so use "nouveau" (not "nouvel"). "Nouvel" is only for masculine nouns starting with a vowel or mute-h. "Nouvelle" is feminine.

grammar.stem: What does "une femme pauvre" mean vs "une pauvre femme"?
options: "Une femme pauvre" = unfortunate woman; "une pauvre femme" = not rich woman
They mean the same thing — position doesn't matter for "pauvre"
"Une femme pauvre" = not rich woman; "une pauvre femme" = unfortunate woman
grammar.rule: Position changes meaning: "pauvre" AFTER the noun = not rich (literally poor). "Pauvre" BEFORE the noun = unfortunate/pitiful. "Une femme pauvre" = a woman without money. "Une pauvre femme" = a poor (unfortunate) woman.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of "beau" before the noun.
grammar.rule: "Hôtel" starts with a mute-h (vowel sound). Before a vowel or mute-h: beau → bel. The pattern is the same as nouveau→nouvel and vieux→vieil.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of "nouveau" before the noun.
grammar.rule: "Ami" starts with a vowel. Before a vowel or mute-h: nouveau → nouvel. Same pattern as beau→bel and vieux→vieil.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of "vieux" before the noun.
grammar.rule: "Château" starts with a consonant (ch-). Before a consonant, use "vieux" (not "vieil"). Vieil is only for masculine nouns starting with a vowel or mute-h.

grammar.stem: Fill in the blank with "joli" in the correct position and form.
grammar.rule: Joli is one of the adjectives that goes BEFORE the noun. Robe is feminine, so joli → jolie (add -e). Une jolie robe.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a beautiful old tree"
grammar.context: arbre (m.) = tree. Use beau/bel and vieux/vieil. Arbre starts with a vowel.
grammar.rule: Arbre starts with a vowel → use "bel" (not "beau"). Both beau and vieux are BANGS adjectives that go before the noun. "Un bel vieil arbre" or "un bel arbre vieux" — either works, though stacking two before the noun is more natural.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "some beautiful houses"
grammar.context: maison (f.) = house. Remember the des → de rule before a preceding adjective.
grammar.rule: Formal French: des → de before a preceding adjective. Beau → belle (fem) → belles (fem pl). De belles maisons. "Des belles maisons" is accepted in spoken French.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "a new old school" (meaning: a school that used to be something else, and the building is ancient)
grammar.context: école (f.) = school. "New" = nouveau (what it became). "Old" = ancien after noun (ancient building). école starts with a vowel.
grammar.rule: Nouveau → nouvelle (feminine, école is f.). "Nouvelle" goes before (BANGS). "Ancienne" after the noun means "ancient/very old." But "ancienne" before means "former." Position matters! "Une nouvelle école ancienne" = a new school that is an old building.

grammar.stem: Why do we say "un bel homme" and not "un beau homme"?
options: Because "homme" is a special noun that always requires "bel" regardless of its starting sound.
Because "beau" changes to "bel" before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or mute-h, to avoid two vowel sounds clashing.
Because "bel" is the formal version of "beau" and is always preferred in writing.
grammar.rule: French avoids the awkward sound of two vowels colliding ("beau homme" → "bo om"). The special form "bel" creates a smooth liaison. Same pattern: nouveau→nouvel, vieux→vieil. This ONLY applies to masculine — feminine "belle" is used regardless.

grammar.stem: Why does "cher" mean "dear" in "mon cher ami" but "expensive" in "un restaurant cher"?
options: Because "cher" is actually two different words that happen to be spelled the same.
Because certain French adjectives change meaning depending on whether they are placed before or after the noun.
Because "cher" before a person is always emotional, and before a thing is always about price.
grammar.rule: Several French adjectives shift meaning with position: cher (before = dear/beloved, after = expensive), ancien (before = former, after = ancient), pauvre (before = unfortunate, after = not rich), propre (before = own, after = clean). It's a single word — position determines meaning.

grammar.stem: What does "sympathique" mean?
grammar.rule: "Sympathique" is a false friend — it means "nice" or "friendly" in French, NOT "sympathetic." Often shortened to "sympa" in spoken French.

grammar.stem: What is the feminine form of "heureux" (happy)?
grammar.rule: Adjectives ending in -eux form their feminine with -euse: heureux → heureuse. Never just add -e to -eux.

grammar.stem: What does "formidable" mean in French?
grammar.rule: "Formidable" in French means "fabulous, terrific, great" — it's positive! In English, "formidable" means intimidating or daunting. Another false friend.

grammar.stem: Which adjective means "stingy"?
grammar.rule: "Avare" means stingy/miserly. "Agréable" means pleasant. "Content(e)" means happy/satisfied. Avare ends in -e, so it's the same for masculine and feminine.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct adjective meaning "tired."
grammar.rule: Fatigué(e) = tired. Feminine form: fatiguée (add -e). The speaker is feminine, so use the feminine agreement.

grammar.stem: Fill in the French adjective meaning "ugly."
grammar.rule: Laid(e) = ugly. Bâtiment is masculine, so use the masculine form: laid. Feminine would be "laide."

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct form of "premier" (first).
grammar.context: C'est la ___ fois (the first time, f.).
grammar.rule: Premier (first) has an irregular feminine: premier → première (-er → -ère). "Fois" is feminine, so use première.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The shy girl is sad."
grammar.context: fille = girl, timide = shy, triste = sad. Both adjectives end in -e.
grammar.rule: Timide and triste both end in silent -e, so they don't change for feminine. They go after the noun (they're not BANGS adjectives). La fille timide est triste.

grammar.stem: Translate into French: "The strong, intelligent woman"
grammar.context: femme = woman, fort(e) = strong, intelligent(e) = intelligent.
grammar.rule: Both adjectives go after the noun (not BANGS). Feminine agreement: fort → forte, intelligent → intelligente. Use "et" (and) to connect them.

grammar.stem: Why does "timide" stay "timide" for both masculine and feminine?
options: Because "timide" is an invariable adjective that never agrees with the noun.
Because adjectives already ending in -e don't add another -e for the feminine — they're already compatible.
Because "timide" is borrowed from English and doesn't follow French rules.
grammar.rule: The -e ending is the feminine marker in French. If an adjective already ends in -e (timide, sincère, sympathique, triste, mince, riche, drôle, facile, difficile), it doesn't need another one. It still changes for plural though: timide → timides.

grammar.stem: Why is "problème" masculine even though it ends in -e?
options: Words borrowed from Greek (like -ème endings) are typically masculine regardless of the final -e
All words ending in -e are masculine in French
Problème changes to feminine when used with a feminine adjective
grammar.rule: Many French words from Greek keep masculine gender despite their -e ending: problème, thème, système, poème. The -e ending does NOT reliably indicate feminine gender.

grammar.stem: Why is "musée" masculine when -ée is usually a feminine ending?
options: The -ée ending is always masculine in French
Musée comes from Greek (mouseion), and Greek-origin -ée words are masculine
Musée is actually feminine — "la musée" is correct
grammar.rule: The -ée ending is usually feminine (une idée, une année, une journée). But Greek-origin words like musée, lycée, and trophée are masculine exceptions. Always learn the article with the noun.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "bijou" (jewel)?
grammar.rule: Bijou is one of 7 special -ou words that take -x in plural: bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou. All other -ou words just add -s.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "travail" (work)?
grammar.rule: Travail → travaux follows the -ail → -aux pattern. Only a few -ail words do this (travail, vitrail, corail, émail). Most -ail words just add -s (détails, éventails).

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "trou" (hole)?
grammar.rule: Trou is a regular -ou word → trous. Only the 7 special -ou words take -x (bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou). Every other -ou word adds -s normally.

grammar.stem: What is the plural of "genou" (knee)?
grammar.rule: Genou is one of the 7 special -ou words that take -x in plural. Mnemonic: "Viens mon chou sur mes genoux avec tes bijoux..."

grammar.rule: Caillou (pebble/stone) is one of the 7 special -ou words → cailloux. Regular -ou words like "clou" just add -s (clous).

grammar.stem: Write the correct plural form of the word in parentheses:
grammar.context: Les ___ (vitrail) de la cathédrale sont magnifiques.
grammar.rule: Vitrail → vitraux follows the -ail → -aux pattern, like travail → travaux. This is a small closed set — most -ail words just add -s.

grammar.stem: Why do "bijou, caillou, genou" take -x in plural while "trou, clou" just take -s?
options: All -ou words take -x in plural; "trou" and "clou" are irregular exceptions
There are exactly 7 special -ou words that take -x; all others follow the regular -s rule
It depends on whether the -ou noun is masculine or feminine
grammar.rule: Only 7 -ou words take -x: bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou. This is a closed, memorized list. Every other -ou word is regular and adds -s.

grammar.stem: Based on its ending, is "situation" masculine or feminine?
grammar.rule: Words ending in -tion are almost always feminine: la situation, la nation, l'information, la réaction, l'éducation.

grammar.stem: Based on its ending, is "appartement" masculine or feminine?
grammar.rule: Words ending in -ment are almost always masculine: le moment, l'appartement, le gouvernement, le sentiment, le mouvement.

grammar.stem: Based on its ending, is "patience" masculine or feminine?
grammar.rule: Words ending in -ence/-ance are almost always feminine: la patience, la danse, l'expérience, l'importance. Notable exception: le silence.

grammar.stem: Based on its ending, is "fromage" masculine or feminine?
grammar.rule: Words ending in -age are almost always masculine: le fromage, le village, le garage, le voyage. Exceptions to watch: la page, la plage, l'image.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct article based on the noun's ending pattern:
grammar.rule: Nation ends in -tion → feminine. The -tion/-sion ending is one of the most reliable feminine markers in French.

grammar.stem: Fill in the correct article based on the noun's ending pattern:
grammar.rule: Moment ends in -ment → masculine. The -ment ending reliably predicts masculine gender.

grammar.stem: Why is "information" feminine in French?
options: Because it describes an abstract concept, and abstract nouns are always feminine
Because the -tion ending is a reliable feminine gender marker in French
Because all long words in French are feminine
grammar.rule: The -tion/-sion ending is one of the strongest feminine predictors. Nearly every -tion word is feminine: l'information, la situation, la nation, l'éducation, la réaction, la conversation.

grammar.stem: Why is "village" masculine in French?
options: Because it ends in -e, and all -e words are masculine
Because all place-related nouns are masculine in French
Because the -age ending is a reliable masculine gender marker
grammar.rule: The -age ending almost always indicates masculine: le village, le garage, le fromage, le voyage. A few exceptions exist (la page, la plage, l'image), but the pattern is very reliable.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):
grammar.context: the tall Italian women grand(e) = tall, italien(ne) = Italian
grammar.rule: Four rules stacked: (1) les — plural definite. (2) grandes — fem pl of grand, BANGS (size) → before noun. (3) femmes — fem pl noun. (4) italiennes — fem pl of italien (double consonant: italien → italienne, +s), nationality → after noun.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):
grammar.context: the happy French boys garçon = boy, heureux = happy
grammar.rule: Three rules stacked: (1) les garçons — masc pl. (2) français — masc pl is same as singular (already ends in -s). (3) heureux — masc pl is same as singular (-eux stays -eux for masculine). Both adjectives after noun in standard position.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):
grammar.context: a good natural reaction réaction (f.) = reaction, naturel = natural
grammar.rule: Four rules stacked: (1) une — fem indefinite (réaction is fem, -tion ending). (2) bonne — fem of bon (double consonant), BANGS → before noun. (3) réaction — fem noun. (4) naturelle — fem of naturel (-el → -elle), descriptive → after noun.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):
grammar.context: the first creative student (f.) premier = first, créatif = creative, étudiant(e) = student
grammar.rule: Four rules stacked: (1) la — fem definite. (2) première — fem of premier (-er → -ère), ordinal → before noun. (3) étudiante — fem of étudiant. (4) créative — fem of créatif (-if → -ive), descriptive → after noun.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):
grammar.context: the generous Italian men homme = man, généreux = generous
grammar.rule: Three rules stacked: (1) les hommes — masc pl. (2) italiens — masc pl of italien (+s). (3) généreux — masc pl stays généreux (-eux no change for masculine plural). Both adjectives after noun.

grammar.stem: Translate to French (apply all agreement and position rules):

grammar.rule: Four rules stacked: (1) des → de before a preceding adjective (formal rule). (2) beaux — irregular masc pl of beau, BANGS (beauty) → before noun. (3) châteaux — château plural (-eau → -eaux). (4) français — masc pl unchanged (ends in -s already), nationality → after noun.

grammar.stem: In "les grandes femmes italiennes," why does "grande" come before the noun but "italienne" comes after?
options: The shorter adjective always goes before, the longer one after
Grande is a BANGS adjective (size) and goes before; italienne is a nationality adjective and goes after
Feminine adjectives go before the noun; plural adjectives go after
grammar.rule: BANGS adjectives (Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, Size) go BEFORE the noun. Most other adjectives — especially nationality, color, and shape — go AFTER. Grande = size (before). Italienne = nationality (after). Length has nothing to do with it.

grammar.stem: In "les garçons heureux," why doesn't "heureux" change form even though it's plural?
options: Adjectives ending in -eux are invariable and never change
Words already ending in -x don't add -s for plural — they already have a plural-compatible ending
"Heureux" is an exception to all agreement rules
grammar.rule: French words ending in -x, -s, or -z don't change in the masculine plural — they already end in a plural-compatible sound. So heureux (sing.) = heureux (pl.), français (sing.) = français (pl.). But the FEMININE forms do change: heureuse → heureuses.

grammar.stem: Translate to French:

grammar.rule: la (maison is feminine) + grande (fem of grand, BANGS/size → before noun) + maison.

grammar.rule: les (plural) + voitures (fem pl of voiture) + rouges (rouge + s for plural, color → after noun). Rouge is one of the adjectives that has the same form for masculine and feminine.

grammar.stem: Translate to French:

grammar.rule: une (fem indefinite) + jeune (BANGS/age → before noun, same form masc/fem) + femme + française (fem of français, nationality → after noun).

questions.q: Comment est la maison de Pierre?

reading.title: Au marché
reading.passage: Marie va au marché. Elle achète des pommes rouges et du fromage français. Le marché est grand et il y a beaucoup de personnes. Les fleurs sont jolies et les gâteaux sont bons. Marie aime le marché parce que les fruits sont frais.

reading.title: L'école de Sophie
reading.passage: L'école de Sophie est nouvelle et moderne. Les salles sont grandes et les fenêtres sont larges. Sophie a un bon professeur français. Il est intelligent et gentil. Les cours sont intéressants mais difficiles. Sophie est une étudiante sérieuse et active.

writing.prompt: Describe your house or apartment in 3-5 sentences.
writing.guidelines: Use definite articles (le/la/les). Include at least 2 adjectives with correct gender agreement. Try to use "il y a" (there is/are). Place adjectives in the correct position (most go after the noun).

writing.prompt: Describe a person you know (family member or friend) in 3-5 sentences.
writing.guidelines: Use être (to be) + adjectives. Include at least one irregular adjective (beau/belle, vieux/vieille, bon/bonne). Make sure all adjectives agree in gender with the person you're describing.
